q.e: Same denominator means same-sized pieces, so just count them: 3 sevenths + 2 sevenths = 5 sevenths. The piece size (7) does not change.
One third of 18 is 18 ÷ 3 = 6; two thirds is 2 × 6 = 12.
The reciprocal is the fraction flipped, because 5/9 × 9/5 = 1.
A quarter of 8 is 2; three quarters is 3 × 2 = 6.
2 wholes = 6 thirds; plus 1 third = 7 thirds.
5 sixths − 1 sixth = 4 sixths. Divide top and bottom by 2: 4/6 = 2/3.
Make the pieces the same size: 3/5 = 21/35 and 4/7 = 20/35. 21 pieces beat 20.
It asks how many halves fit in 6. Each whole has 2 halves, so 6 × 2 = 12.
The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6. Dividing both by 6 gives 2/3. (6/9 and 4/6 are equal to it but not fully reduced.)
It means half of a third. Cut a third into 2 equal parts and each part is one sixth of the whole.
LCM of 3 and 4 is 12: 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12. Never add the denominators — the piece size must match first.
Change to improper fractions: 7/2 × 16/7. The 7s cancel, leaving 16/2 = 8.
Dividing by a fraction = multiplying by its reciprocal: 4/5 × 15/8 = 60/40 = 3/2 = 1 1/2.

q.t: How many hours are there in 3/8 of a day?
q.e: A day has 24 hours. One eighth is 3 hours, so three eighths is 9 hours.
12/5 ÷ 6 = 12/5 × 1/6 = 12/30 = 2/5. Sharing 12 fifths among 6 gives 2 fifths each.

q.t: A fraction is multiplied by its reciprocal. What is the product?
q.e: a/b × b/a: the top and bottom are the same number (ab), so the product is always 1.
In sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1 whole.

q.t: Cloth costs ₹48 per metre. What is the cost of 3 3/4 m (in ₹)?
A rope 11 m long is cut into pieces each 2 3/4 m long. How many pieces are there?
q.e: 11 ÷ 11/4 = 11 × 4/11 = 4. Division asks how many pieces of that size fit.

q.t: A book has 150 pages. Rina reads 2/5 of it on day one, and 1/3 of the REMAINING pages on day two. How many pages are left?
q.e: Day one: 2/5 of 150 = 60, leaving 90. Day two: 1/3 of 90 = 30, leaving 60. The second fraction is of what is left, not of 150.

q.t: Find the area of a rectangle 5 1/3 m long and 2 1/4 m wide (in m²).
q.e: Area = length × breadth = 16/3 × 9/4. Cancel: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so 4 × 3 = 12.

q.t: By what number should 3 3/4 be multiplied to get 5?
q.e: Undo the multiplication by dividing: 5 ÷ 15/4 = 5 × 4/15 = 20/15 = 4/3 = 1 1/3.

q.t: A car runs 16 2/3 km on 1 litre of petrol. How far does it go on 2 2/5 litres (in km)?
The sum of two fractions is 5 1/6. One of them is 2 3/4. Find the other.

q.e: ‘Of’ means multiply. 2/3 of 240 = 160, then 3/4 of 160 = 120. (Or 3/4 × 2/3 = 1/2, and half of 240 is 120.)

q.t: Which of these fractions is the largest?
q.e: With denominator 48: 2/3 = 32/48, 5/8 = 30/48, 7/12 = 28/48, 9/16 = 27/48. The biggest numerator wins.

q.t: A tank is 3/5 full and holds 420 litres at that level. What is its full capacity (in litres)?
q.e: 3 fifths = 420, so 1 fifth = 140 and the whole (5 fifths) = 700.
Each term splits: 1/(1×2) = 1 − 1/2, 1/(2×3) = 1/2 − 1/3, and so on. The middle parts cancel, leaving 1 − 1/5 = 4/5.

q.t: A man spends 1/3 of his salary on rent, 1/4 on food and 1/6 on travel. He saves the remaining ₹6000. What is his salary (in ₹)?
q.e: Spent: 4/12 + 3/12 + 2/12 = 9/12 = 3/4. So 1/4 of the salary is ₹6000 and the whole is 4 × 6000 = ₹24000.

q.t: The numerator of a fraction is 4 less than its denominator. If 1 is added to both, the fraction becomes 1/2. What is the fraction?
q.e: Test it: 3/7 has numerator 4 less than denominator, and (3+1)/(7+1) = 4/8 = 1/2 ✓. The others fail the second condition.

q.t: A pole has 1/4 of its length in mud and 2/5 in water. The remaining 7 m is above the water. How long is the pole (in m)?
q.e: In mud and water: 5/20 + 8/20 = 13/20. So 7/20 of the pole is 7 m, 1/20 is 1 m, and the pole is 20 m.

q.t: A ball always bounces back to 2/3 of the height it fell from. It is dropped from 54 m. How high does it rise after the 3rd bounce (in m)?
q.e: Each bounce multiplies the height by 2/3: 54 → 36 → 24 → 16.

q.t: How many packets of 3/8 kg can be filled from 7 1/2 kg of sugar?
Which of these fractions lies between 1/3 and 1/2?
q.e: In twelfths, 1/3 = 4/12 and 1/2 = 6/12. Only 5/12 sits between them (1/4 = 3/12 and 2/3 = 8/12 are outside).

q.t: Half of a number is 12 more than one-fifth of the same number. Find the number.
q.e: 1/2 − 1/5 = 3/10 of the number equals 12, so 1/10 is 4 and the number is 40. Check: 20 − 8 = 12 ✓.

q.t: A tap fills 1/6 of a tank every hour, but a leak empties 1/15 of the tank every hour. How many hours does the tank take to fill?
q.e: Net filling each hour = 1/6 − 1/15 = 5/30 − 2/30 = 3/30 = 1/10 of the tank, so 10 hours fill it.
